Let’s dive into Chapter 5: The Culture of Questioning and the Value of Failure.
In a lot of places around the world, challenging authority is risky business. Most of us grow up hearing that we should respect our elders, stick to the rules, and avoid rocking the boat. But in Israel, things couldn’t be more different. From a really young age, kids are encouraged to ask questions, to argue their point, and to push back against what’s always been done.
This isn’t just a quirky cultural detail—it’s actually one of Israel’s biggest strengths.
It all starts at home. Parents expect their kids to speak up, to defend their ideas—even if that means challenging mom or dad. Then at school, teachers don’t just allow debate, they invite it. They want students to challenge their own assumptions and even question the teacher’s point of view.
And when you get to the military, things don’t change. Junior officers are supposed to question their superiors if they see a better way to get things done. This habit of thinking critically and speaking up? It doesn’t stop at the classroom or the army—it follows people right into the workplace. Meetings can get loud, debates are common, and disagreements just show that folks are engaged—not that they’re being disrespectful.
Here’s a story that really shows what this looks like. Imagine a team of engineers facing a problem that seems totally unsolvable. They spend hours arguing over possible solutions. Voices get loud, tempers flare—nobody backs down. But in the end, the best idea wins. And it’s not because the most senior person came up with it. It wins because it survived the toughest questions and the harshest scrutiny. Sure, the process is messy, but it works.
Now, this willingness to challenge authority goes hand in hand with an unusual attitude toward failure. In Israel, trying and failing isn’t something to be ashamed of—it’s actually a badge of honor. If you’ve started a company and watched it fall apart, people respect you for the experience you’ve picked up along the way. Investors are even more likely to back someone who’s failed before, because they know you’ve learned some valuable lessons.
Most people don’t realize how rare this mindset is. In a lot of cultures, failure is something you hide, or even deny. But in Israel, it’s just part of the journey. The country’s most successful entrepreneurs? Many of them have a handful of failed ventures behind them. They’re open about their mistakes and eager to share what they’ve learned.
This openness creates a special kind of psychological safety. People feel comfortable taking risks, trying out new things, and admitting when they’re wrong. And because of that, innovation really takes off. New ideas get tested quickly, and the bad ones are tossed aside without any regret. The goal is always to learn and keep moving forward.
So, here’s the key takeaway. When people are free to question, to argue, and yes, to fail—they become more creative, more resilient, and way more willing to take the kinds of risks that lead to big breakthroughs. In Israel, this culture of questioning and embracing failure sits right at the heart of the country’s success.
